Por isso, consideramos o acento de intensidade imprevisível, ora incindindo sobre a primeira sílaba da raiz dos substantivos e verbos, ora sobre a segunda, não havendo nenhuma evidência de condicionamento fonológico. Por essa razão não formulamos nenhuma regra de acentuação; o acento de intensidade deve ser especificado no léxico. new_statements.translation: Although the Griffiths (1976:144) state that stress is predictable in Kadiwéu, we found no confirmation of this claim in the data we collected. We therefore consider intensity stress unpredictable, falling sometimes on the first syllable of the root of nouns and verbs, sometimes on the second, with no evidence of phonological conditioning. For this reason we formulate no stress rule; intensity stress must be specified in the lexicon. [Griffiths & Griffiths 1976:144:] In general the stressed syllables correspond to the first high-tone syllable within the word, in the case of nouns and verbs [high tone occurring on the first syllable of the verb or noun root and on utterance-penultimate syllables, §6.4].

new_statements.rule_in_words: The two accessible first-hand descriptions disagree: Griffiths & Griffiths (1976) tie stress to a morphophonemic 'high tone' on the root-initial syllable of nouns and verbs (root-initial prominence, plus utterance-penultimate high tone), while Braggio (1981) finds stress lexically unpredictable, on either the first or the second syllable of the root, marked phonetically by lengthening of the stressed syllable's onset consonant. A native-speaker MA (Pires 2022) likewise says the tonic syllable is the first or second syllable of the word, with post-tonic vowel lengthening. The modern reference analysis (Sandalo 1995/1997, metrical feet, dialect-dependent) could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in Braggio or Griffiths. Griffiths note utterance-level falling intonation/intensity that strengthens initial and weakens final syllables (§9.1, p.152) and high tone on utterance-penultimate syllables (§6.4).
new_statements.exceptions: Griffiths: stress/high tone apparently absent on nominal and verbal modifiers; high-tone placement can be masked by intonation. Braggio: no conditioning found; stress lexical. Pires 2022: stress shifts from 1st to 2nd syllable in the 'humble' (post-mourning) speech register; Souza 2012 (after Sandalo 1995:39): noble and non-noble sociolects have different stress/foot systems.
new_statements.domain_note: Braggio and Griffiths speak of the root of nouns and verbs within the word (isolated words and short utterances); Griffiths' 'tom alto' rule (iii) is utterance-level (penultimate syllable of the enunciado). Pires speaks of the word (loanwords in citation form).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Kadiwéu (kadi1248) of the Bodoquena area, Mato Grosso do Sul. Note sociolectal split: Sandalo 1995 (per Souza 2012) is based on non-noble Kadiwéu and reports a different stress/foot system for noble Kadiwéu; Pires 2022 reports stress shift in the 'humble' register. Griffiths' data are mainly male speech.
